title: Winston Churchill and the Novice Member of Parliament: Words as Weapons in Westminster
summary: In the corridors of Westminster, veteran statesman Winston Churchill offered unforgettable advice to an anxious rookie MP on how to master the spoken word in debate.
full_text:
In the early 1950s, inside the Members' Cloakroom of the British House of Commons, a newly elected young Member of Parliament was pacing nervously before delivering his maiden speech.

Catching sight of Prime Minister Winston Churchill, the anxious newcomer approached the veteran orator:
"Mr. Churchill, sir, I confess I am terrified. As I look across the floor of the chamber at the benches opposite, I see a wall of hostile faces. How does one endure the venom of so many political enemies?"

Churchill took a slow draw on his cigar, his eyes twinkling with mischievous amusement:
"My dear boy, you are committing a fundamental constitutional error! Those honourable gentlemen sitting opposite you on the opposition benches are not your enemies. They are merely the political Opposition!
If you wish to discover your real enemies, turn your head and look behind you on your own government backbenches! That is where your true rivals sit, patiently measuring the size of your boots and calculating how soon you might fall!"

Churchill then gripped the young man's arm and added with paternal warmth:
"Remember two golden rules at the dispatch box: First, never use two adjectives where one noun will suffice. Cultivate the habit of eating your own words—I have frequently done so in my long career, and I have always found them to be an exceptionally wholesome and nutritious diet! Second, never shout to compensate for weak logic. Speak plainly, speak truthfully, and let the facts do the fighting."

Disarmed by Churchill's wit, the young MP walked into the chamber with newfound composure and delivered a sparkling address.
